proposals.name: The Mung
proposals.entry:
The Mung are one of the four great powers of the 99 War: four-foot, blue-gray, bald-headed people with shaggy shoulders and limbs, broad hands, bulldog faces, sharp teeth, and lean blocky bodies. They are numerous, fast-growing, relentlessly practical, and unnervingly alike.

They make no songs, stories, paintings, jokes, written language, heirlooms, or monuments to individual lives. They regard commemoration as a costly distraction.

The Great Multiplication

Mung settlements are dense fields of dried mud brick: nurseries, ration courts, iron pits, drill yards, and shared sleeping chambers. Their people mature quickly and recover population with alarming speed.

War Without Glory

Mung equipment is basic black iron: round helmets, tall rectangular shields, spears, hooks, axes, and stout spring-iron bows firing cheap one-piece cast arrows. They have no guns, artillery schools, knightly orders, or celebrated captains. Flags, horn blasts, moving standards, and task-marks direct them.

Their doctrine is Expenditure: bodies and labor substitute for costly craft. They cross marshes, fill trenches, breach walls, and continue a charge after other armies would call its price impossible. Their weakness is imagination: false routes, hidden mechanisms, broken supply rhythms, and impossible choices can defeat a host built to solve literal problems.

Marks Instead of Writing

The geometric brands on Mung helmets and left breasts are not letters. They identify task, breeding-house, and ration priority. A Mung reassigned from bridge-building to siege labor receives a new mark and ceases to be what it was.

War Barges

Mung fleets are giant, low black war barges—broad mud-water hulls crowded with infantry, poles, shields, grain paste, iron, and the equipment to unload an army into a floodplain. They are floating workyards, not elegant ships.

The Golden God

The Mung’s only representational art is the Golden God, a colossal hollow golden skull-head carried above the host on hundreds of poles. Its deep hollow eyes, hard geometric muzzle, and square teeth are the holy sign of the Mung. At the decisive moment, a war host may hurl the Golden God into the enemy line, then push it over the fallen. The god’s purpose is to move forward.

Fogport Hooks

  • A Mung work-host has bought a derelict warehouse and begun excavating below it, using poles too long to fit through any door.
  • Hundreds of Mung children arrive without soldiers; the Civic Order wants them confined, while their caretaker insists they are neither cargo nor prisoners.
  • A piece of hammered gold from the Golden God circulates through the Shambles, and Mung laborers begin appearing outside whoever carries it.
